title: Indexed Singly Linked List
statement:
Build your own linked list that supports positions (0-based indexes). Do not use a built-in list type for the storage in the version an interviewer expects; a node chain is the point.

  • IndexedList() creates an empty list.
  • get(index) returns the value at index, or -1 if the index is out of range.
  • addAtHead(val) puts val before the first element.
  • addAtTail(val) puts val after the last element.
  • addAtIndex(index, val) inserts val so that it ends up at position index. If index equals the length, it is appended. If index is larger than the length, nothing happens.
  • deleteAtIndex(index) removes the element at index if that index exists; otherwise nothing happens.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the list. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: The list goes [5] → [5, 9] → [5, 7, 9]. Position 1 holds 7. Deleting position 0 leaves [7, 9].
Index 1 on an empty list is past the end, so 4 is ignored. Index 0 inserts 2, and index 1 then equals the length, so 3 is appended.

hints: Almost every operation needs the node just before some position. Write that walk once.
A dummy node in front of the real head means inserting or deleting at index 0 is no longer a special case.
Keep a size counter so you can reject bad indexes before walking. Then insert at index i = walk i steps from the dummy and splice after it; delete works the same way.

explain.intuition:
A singly linked list can only reach position i by walking from the front, so every operation boils down to "find the node just before position i, then rewire one pointer". Head and tail insertions are the cases i = 0 and i = size.

The trouble spots are the edges: inserting before the first node or deleting the first node changes the head itself. A sentinel node that always sits in front of the real head removes those special cases, because every real node then has a predecessor. A size counter lets you reject bad indexes in O(1). It is the same trick as a wrapper element around a list in the DOM: you always have a parent to call insertBefore on.
steps: Keep a sentinel node dummy whose next is the first real node, and a size counter.
get(i): if i ≥ size return -1; otherwise walk i + 1 steps from dummy and return that value.
addAtIndex(i, v): if i > size do nothing. Otherwise walk i steps from dummy to the predecessor, splice in a new node after it, and increase size.
deleteAtIndex(i): if i ≥ size do nothing. Otherwise walk to the predecessor, set pred.next = pred.next.next, decrease size.
pitfalls: Treating addAtIndex with index = size as invalid. It must append.
Keeping a separate tail pointer and forgetting to move it back after deleting the last node. Then the next addAtTail attaches to a node that is no longer in the list.
Walking one step too far or too few: the insert and delete walks stop at the predecessor, while get stops at the node itself.

complexity.time: O(i) per operation at index i; O(1) for addAtHead

solutions.title: Array-backed
solutions.idea: Store values in a dynamic array and let splice do the shifting. Fine in practice, but it skips what the question tests.

solutions.title: Singly linked list with a sentinel
solutions.idea: A dummy node in front of the head and a size counter. Every operation walks to the predecessor of the target position.

followups: Make addAtTail O(1) with a tail pointer. Which operations now have to keep it up to date?
Switch to a doubly linked list. How can get(i) walk from whichever end is closer?
